title: Small volumes to two decimal places for infants and children
blurb: Round small children's volumes correctly to two decimal places: look at the third digit, round once at the end, keep the leading zero.
question: A child is prescribed 70 mg of a medicine. The oral suspension is labelled 120 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given, to two decimal places?

teach.body: Formal rule: to round to two decimal places, look at the third decimal digit; if it is 5 or more, add one to the second digit, otherwise leave it, then drop everything after the second digit. Plain English: keep hundredths, and let the thousandths decide. The children's practice paper asked for two decimal places on several liquid volumes, and Pearson marks only the exact rounded figure.
teach.cite: Pearson VUE NMC children's practice paper; FACTS.md section 5 (rounding)

teach.h: Worked example: Ruby in a children's assessment unit
teach.body: Ruby, 3, is prescribed 70 mg; the suspension is 120 mg/5 mL. Volume = 70 ÷ 120 × 5 = 2.916666… mL. The third decimal is 6, so round up: 2.92 mL. Sense-check: 70 mg is a bit over half of 120 mg, so a bit over half of 5 mL. You type 2.92 mL.

teach.h: Four ways to lose the mark

teach.text: Rounding too early: rounding the fraction (70 ÷ 120 = 0.583 → 0.6) or the dose before multiplying moves the final volume. Keep the full calculator value and round once, at the very end.

teach.caption: Pearson's practice engine used conventional half-up rounding (5 rounds up).

teach.body: Small doses are drawn up in 1 mL oral syringes, so a difference of 0.05 mL matters. In the exam, write the figure the instruction asks for: two decimal places means two digits after the point, with a leading zero for values below 1.
teach.cite: Pearson VUE NMC practice tests, answer-format guidance

items: Look at the third decimal digit: 5 or more rounds up.
Round once, at the end; never round the fraction or the dose first.
Leading zero below 1 (0.86), no extra trailing zeros.
Two decimal places is not one: 2.9 loses the mark when 2.92 is asked.

summary: You can now round children's liquid volumes to exactly two decimal places using the third digit, round only once at the end, and type the result with a leading zero and no extra zeros.

A.q: A child is prescribed 75 mg of a medicine. The oral suspension is labelled 120 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.
A.why: 75 ÷ 120 × 5 = 3.125. The third decimal is 5, so round up: 3.13 mL.

whyNot.0: Truncated: a third decimal of 5 rounds up.
whyNot.2: Rounded 0.625 to 0.63 before multiplying: rounding too early.

A.q: A child is prescribed 43 mg of a medicine. The oral suspension is labelled 250 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.
A.why: 43 ÷ 250 × 5 = 0.86 mL exactly, typed with a leading zero.

whyNot.0: Forgot to multiply by the 5 mL stock volume.
whyNot.1: Rounded to one decimal place; the stem asks for two.

A.q: A baby weighing 3.8 kg is prescribed a medicine at 15 mg/kg. The oral suspension is labelled 120 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.
A.why: Dose = 15 × 3.8 = 57 mg. Volume = 57 ÷ 120 × 5 = 2.375. Third decimal 5 rounds up: 2.38 mL.

whyNot.1: Truncated: a third decimal of 5 rounds up.
whyNot.3: Forgot to multiply by the 5 mL stock volume.

B.q: A child weighing 7.3 kg is prescribed a medicine at 7.5 mg/kg. The oral suspension is labelled 100 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.

whyNot.0: Truncated: the third decimal (7) should round up.
whyNot.1: Rounded the dose to 55 mg first: rounding too early.

B.q: A child is prescribed 62.5 mg of a medicine. The oral solution is labelled 40 mg/mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.

whyNot.2: Multiplied by 5 as if the label were per 5 mL.

B.q: A child is prescribed 9 mg of a medicine. The oral solution is labelled 100 mg/5 mL, so the volume to give is 0.45 mL. The answer box asks for the correct unit and two decimal places. Which entry would be marked correct?
B.why: 9 ÷ 100 × 5 = 0.45 mL. The correct entry has a leading zero and exactly two decimal places: 0.45 mL.

whyNot.0: Missing the leading zero; ".9 mL" was marked wrong on the practice test.
whyNot.1: Three decimal places: an extra trailing zero.

C.q: A child weighing 13.6 kg is prescribed a medicine at 20 mg/kg/day in three divided doses. The oral suspension is labelled 250 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given for each dose? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.

whyNot.0: Rounded the dose to 91 mg first: rounding too early.

C.q: A child weighing 9.2 kg is prescribed a medicine at 150 micrograms/kg. The oral solution is labelled 1 mg/mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.

whyNot.0: No conversion: micrograms treated as mg.
whyNot.3: Forgot to multiply by the weight.

C.q: A child weighing 16 kg is prescribed a medicine at 4 mg/kg. The oral suspension is labelled 30 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.

whyNot.1: Truncated: the third decimal (6) should round up.
whyNot.3: Forgot to multiply by the 5 mL stock volume.

reteach.title: Let the third digit decide
reteach.question: Your calculator shows 1.6666667. What is that to two decimal places?

blocks.body: 1.66|66667: the third decimal is 6, which is 5 or more, so the second digit goes up: 1.67. Cutting it off at 1.66 is truncating, and it is marked wrong.

blocks.text: Do not round twice. Rounding 1.666 to 1.7 and then writing 1.70 is both the wrong value and a trailing zero.

explain.body: Rounding looks at the next digit. Truncating just chops. 1.667 rounds to 1.67; truncating gives 1.66.

test.q: A child is prescribed 5 mg of a medicine. The oral solution is labelled 3 mg/mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.
test.why: 5 ÷ 3 = 1.6666… The third decimal is 6, so 1.67 mL.

test.q: A child is prescribed 37 mg of a medicine. The oral suspension is labelled 120 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.

whyNot.0: Rounded 0.3083 to 0.31 before multiplying: rounding too early.
whyNot.3: Forgot to multiply by the 5 mL stock volume.

test.q: A child is prescribed 21 mg of a medicine. The oral suspension is labelled 40 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.
test.why: 21 ÷ 40 × 5 = 2.625. A third decimal of 5 rounds up: 2.63 mL.

whyNot.0: Truncated: a third decimal of 5 rounds up.
whyNot.3: Forgot to multiply by the 5 mL stock volume.

explain.body: Below 1 mL, always type the zero before the point: 0.33 mL. It is required, and it makes the decimal point impossible to miss.

test.q: A child is prescribed 3.3 mg of a medicine. The oral solution is labelled 10 mg/mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.
test.why: 3.3 ÷ 10 = 0.33 mL, typed with its leading zero.

whyNot.3: Multiplied by 5 as if the label were per 5 mL.
